problems.description: Wholesale replacement of the existing Flask Todo API — the entire seed app (models, routes, error handling) is deleted and replaced with an async WebSocket server, discarding prior functionality with no coexistence, migration, or deprecation path; a 'greenfield' session does not justify destroying the seed's public surface.
messages.py: 'ValueError(f"invalid JSON message")' uses an f-string with no interpolated variables — a pointless f-string the compiler will flag.
Mechanical convention score 0.79 with 19 violations, e.g. module-level constants not UPPER_CASE in app.py, broker.py, rate_limit.py and PascalCase/snake_case complaints in __init__.py re-exports.
No tests accompany the new notification package — message envelope parsing, client registry, and server lifecycle are all untested at session 1.

strengths: Well-decomposed package layout (messages, registry, server, broker, rate_limit) with clear separation of concerns rather than a single monolithic file.
Consistent typing and docstrings on all public signatures; envelope shape and SUPPORTED_TYPES validation in messages.py are sound.
Thread-safe ClientRegistry with unique-ID mapping is a sensible foundation for concurrent WebSocket connections.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid greenfield package architecture for a WebSocket notification server, but achieved by erasing the existing Flask API rather than extending it, landing a neutral outcome with a modest convention score (0.79) and minor lint/maintainability nits.

problems.description: Registry.subscriber_count() and channels() expose count-based views that the server never uses (server uses channel_members() for routing); subscriber_count in particular is dead/speculative API surface.

Partial DRY refactor: the new _json_response() helper is used for /health, /channels, and history endpoints, but the 404 NOT_FOUND response still hand-rolls the same Response construction with a hardcoded Content-Length "9", leaving an inconsistency in the same method.

subscribe/unsubscribe are acknowledged only on error; a successful subscription gets no confirmation envelope, so a client cannot distinguish 'subscribed' from 'dropped mid-flight' without inspecting registry state.

strengths: Backward-compatible extension of the message envelope: the channel field is optional, and broadcast-without-channel retains its existing all-clients semantics (verified by test_message_without_channel_still_broadcasts_to_all).
All new registry methods (subscribe/unsubscribe/channel_members/is_subscribed) acquire the existing threading.Lock and return snapshots, preserving the module's stated thread-safety contract.
Lifecycle hygiene: unregister() removes the client from every channel and prunes empty channels, and a disconnect-cleanup test covers it.
Substantial test suite — 167 lines / 8 tests covering channel routing, unsubscribe, multi-channel, REST endpoints (/channels, /channels/<name>/subscribers), and error paths; 33 tests pass.
Clean static-method extraction (_json_response) consolidates repetitive response construction, and validation in make_message/parse_message matches the established raise-ValueError pattern.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-tested channel-subscription feature that extends the existing envelope schema and registry patterns cleanly — the 0.79 measured convention score is whole-repo and stems almost entirely from pre-existing violations in files untouched by this diff (app.py, broker.py, rate_limit.py, __init__.py), plus an apparent false positive on messages.py, which contains no classes.

problems.description: Persisted client-state keys (instance:<id>, channel_members:<channel>, client_channels:<id>) carry no TTL and are only removed on clean disconnect. A crashed server instance leaves orphaned membership state in the restart-survival store, undermining the multi-instance/survives-restart property the session spec explicitly requires.
default_broker() docstring claims a warning on fakeredis fallback, but no warning is emitted — the doc/code contract is out of sync.
fakeredis is imported into the production broker path as a silent no-Redis fallback, masking missing infrastructure and letting tests pass against a fake that diverges from real Redis behavior.

Package-wide convention score of 0.79 with 19 naming violations (app.py/messages.py/rate_limit.py PascalCase + UPPER_CASE; __init__.py/broker.py). Note the new broker.py itself is clean — most flags are pre-existing session-1/2 code or regex false positives (e.g. the re-export-only __init__.py contains no def/class lines).

strengths: RedisBroker is a clean, namespaced pub/sub abstraction (broadcast/channel:<name>/instance:<id>) that directly implements the session-3 spec and supports multiple server instances over one backbone.
Backward-compatible extension of ClientRegistry.register() to accept externally allocated IDs, preserving local uniqueness as fallback — respects existing callers.
Async-safe close() handling both aclose() and close() so real and fake Redis clients clean up correctly.
New modules (broker.py, store.py) consistently wired into package __init__.py exports following the established package pattern.
Env-driven config (REDIS_URL) with a testable fakeredis fallback, plus full type hints and docstrings on the public API.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, spec-conforming Redis-backbone integration with clean abstraction and backward-compatible extension, though the measured 0.79 convention score is partly inflated by heuristic false positives and the commit carries real debt from un-TTL'd restart-state keys.

problems.description: The new transport abstraction (BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport/default_transport, +194 lines, 2 new classes) ships with no dedicated tests; it is exercised only indirectly via the existing integration tests running on the default WebSocket path, leaving the env-var selection and the abstract contract unverified.

Registry type safety regressed: ClientRegistry._clients changed from dict[str, ServerConnection] to dict[str, Any] (also get()/register()/__iter__). A Generic[Conn] parameter would preserve static typing while staying transport-agnostic.

The 'pluggable' boundary is partially leaky: WebSocketTransport reaches back into server privates (_register_connection, _unregister_connection, _route, _process_request) and reads server.registry, and BaseTransport.process_request delegates to the server's REST handler which still uses websockets.http11.Request/Response types — so a non-HTTP transport is not actually drop-in.

Untyped parameters in the new surface: WebSocketTransport.__init__(server, ...) drops the server annotation, and _process_request/_register_connection take untyped `connection` (previously annotated ServerConnection).
WebSocketTransport.bound_port indexes self._server.sockets[0] and will raise AttributeError if read before start(); NotificationServer.bound_port now forwards to it unconditionally.

strengths: Clean Adapter/Strategy extraction: the server core is now transport-agnostic, with all outbound delivery and the socket lifecycle moved behind BaseTransport.
Consistent with existing DI conventions — the default_transport factory mirrors default_broker/default_store/default_rate_limit, and transport is constructor-injected alongside broker and store.
Behavior-preserving refactor: all 75 existing tests pass and message routing semantics are unchanged.
Well-documented module/class docstrings, snake_case methods, PascalCase classes, and __all__ exports updated in __init__.py.
Env-var transport selection (TRANSPORT) with graceful fallback to the default WebSocket transport.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, behavior-preserving Adapter refactor that decouples the notification core from WebSocket and follows existing DI patterns, though it erases registry type safety, ships the new abstraction untested, and retains a slightly leaky transport boundary — the 0.79 convention score mostly reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (app.py, broker.py, messages.py, rate_limit.py), so this commit's own delta is cleaner than the measurement suggests.

problems.description: RedisBroker.client property (broker.py) exposes the private _client, leaking internal state and tightening server-to-broker coupling; the rate limiter reaches through the broker instead of receiving the client as a constructor dependency.

Mechanical score 0.79 with 19 flagged violations, but the listed items (PascalCase classes, snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE constants in __init__.py/app.py/broker.py) appear spurious — the actual new code (RateLimiter, default_rate_limit, etc.) uses correct casing. Discrepancy between the static measurement and a manual read of the diff.

`except (asyncio.CancelledError, Exception)` in close() is redundant — CancelledError derives from BaseException in Python 3.8+, and the broad `except Exception` already swallows real cleanup errors, masking shutdown failures.

RateLimiter.check uses incr-then-expire without locking, so counter creation is not atomic across concurrent calls — a fixed-window (not true rolling) approximation. Acceptable for the story context but worth documenting.

strengths: Rate limit module mirrors the established default-factory + env-var config pattern (default_store/default_broker), and is exported via __init__.py consistently with the package conventions.
Redis-backed shared counters correctly enforce the limit across all server instances sharing a backbone and survive restarts — architecturally sound placement in the messaging layer.
Async check/reset API and namespace-scoped keys match the codebase's existing async patterns and broker namespace conventions.
commit_reviews.summary: Adds a well-integrated Redis-backed rate limiter and history/cleanup plumbing that follows the package's default-factory patterns, slightly marred by a broker encapsulation leak, a redundant exception clause, and a convention score (0.79) whose listed violations appear to be static-analysis noise rather than real casing errors.

compounding_issues: README frozen at session 1 — never updated for channels, Redis, transport, rate limiting, or history endpoints; doc drift compounds across all 5 sessions

Transport abstraction (session 4) is only partially applied: _handle_message still takes a raw websockets.WebSocketServerProtocol and calls websocket.send directly, and session 5 embeds rate limiting inside that WebSocket-coupled handler, entrenching the coupling the refactor was meant to remove
Repo hygiene debt: __pycache__/*.pyc and messages.db binaries committed in every session, accumulating noise in each commit
Deprecated websockets API (WebSocketServerProtocol) persists through the final state, producing warnings in every test run
key_decisions: Session 1 monolithic app.py with global singletons (ClientRegistry, MessageDatabase, RedisBroker) that everything later accretes onto

Session 3: adopting Redis pub/sub as the message backbone plus SQLite persistence in dedicated modules (database.py, redis_broker.py) — the load-bearing choice; session 5's Redis-counter rate limiting and history endpoints both build directly on it
Session 4: pluggable transport layer (BaseTransport ABC, WebSocketTransport, get_transport factory driven by TRANSPORT env var)
Consistent test-heavy incremental delivery: test suite grew 20→33→58→76→107 alongside code (199→302→747→1169→1339 lines), green at every commit, with ~1.5 test:code ratio
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the arc. Each session landed with a fully passing suite (20, 33, 58, 76, then 106 passed), and the architecture matured visibly: sessions 3-4 introduced real modularity (separate database, redis_broker, and transport modules) in place of session 1's single-file monolith. Session 5 — the largest and hardest, with 5 retries and a 606-line test addition — was the cleanest landing, extending the existing Redis/SQLite infrastructure rather than reworking it, which signals the earlier modularization paid off. The arc is marred only by non-functional debt: the README stopped being maintained after session 1, the transport refactor left the message-handling core still WebSocket-bound, and committed binaries plus deprecated API usage accumulated throughout.
story_review.summary: A coherent, green-at-every-step five-session progression where the session-3 Redis/SQLite backbone cleanly supports the final cross-cutting work, held back only by a stale README and a partially-applied transport abstraction.
